stories.headline: Anthropic publishes a Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, machine-checked but unread by any mathematician
stories.why_read: A repo that claims RH and GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, checked by Lean's kernel, with the authors themselves saying no human has read it through.
body: A repository from Anthropic titled "A short Lean 4 proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis" holds a Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The README says the proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, written with Claude, and that this repository is a shorter version produced with colleagues at Anthropic and Claude. It ships in two editions: a readable one of about 300,000 lines and a compact one of about 76,000 lines covering the same five theorems.

The caveats are in the authors' own words: it is a research artifact, not maintained, and "the proof has passed machine checks only." The README states that no mathematician has read it through and that no paper comes with it. A build needs Lean v4.35.0 and a pinned Mathlib commit and takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory. The code is Apache 2.0 licensed, and the repo had 716 stars when checked. The HN thread drew roughly 480 points.

stories.headline: A back-of-envelope case for orbital AI: $3M satellite, 175 kW of compute, $250/kg launch, 57% gross margin
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd and bookmarked this one: a short, checkable calculation of why SpaceX thinks compute in orbit can pencil out.
body: James Cat (@TSLAFanMtl) lays out "very conservative" assumptions: each satellite costs SpaceX $3M to build and averages 175 kW of compute; launch costs $250/kg for a 3-tonne satellite, or $0.75M; useful life is 5 years. That is $3.75M to get one operational, or $750k a year. Selling compute at $10B per gigawatt-year would earn $1.75M a year per satellite, a 57% gross margin, and the arithmetic holds.

The inputs are his, not SpaceX's. He says today's compute rates are $30-50B per GW-year and that SpaceX is targeting $10/kg with Starship v4, versus about $1,000/kg for Falcon today, and he concludes that Starship makes an "insurmountable moat." Treat it as an advocate's model, not a forecast, but it is a clean way to see which numbers matter: launch price per kilogram and the price of compute.

stories.headline: Scott Aaronson: AI proofs are now answering decades-old complexity questions outright
stories.why_read: The sharpest first-person reaction yet from a complexity theorist to this week's run of AI-produced results.
body: On Shtetl-Optimized, Aaronson says OpenAI and Anthropic have produced proofs that VP ≠ VNP, following the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and that OpenAI now claims the matrix-multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4, with a lower bound matching the upper bound OpenAI proved in its October 6 drop. He calls the real shock that an AI proved any bound of the form ω > 2.

He also cites an OpenAI release claiming the number of linear gates needed for the Fourier Transform is N(log N)^(1/2+o(1)), with a matching lower bound, and notes Yupan Liu's QIP(2) = PSPACE preprint, where AI help barely raised an eyebrow. His conclusion: expect "a whole new continent of mathematical truth," not one-off solutions. These are his reading of claims that are still being checked.

stories.headline: Tesla Robotaxi and Waymo price-matched on a 2-mile Dallas ride, and a Cybercab option appears
stories.why_read: A rider's side-by-side on Thanksgiving eve, which is about as real-world as robotaxi pricing gets.
body: Abhimanyu Yadav (@WorldlyReviewer) posted screenshots comparing a 2-mile trip in Dallas on Thanksgiving eve: Tesla Robotaxi and Waymo were "basically price matched," with Uber higher. He added that Uber prices in Austin being so low is, he bets, because of Waymo.

He also said it was exciting to see a Cybercab option in Dallas "after so long." This is one rider's screenshot on one day, with holiday-eve demand, so it is anecdote rather than a pricing study. Anand RT'd and bookmarked it.

stories.headline: SpaceX cuts Nvidia Blackwell rental prices on smaller clusters to $10-$12 per GPU-hour
stories.why_read: Compute pricing is the clearest read on whether AI capacity is tightening or easing.
body: According to X's news summary of posts, SpaceX lowered spot rates for Nvidia Blackwell GPUs on smaller clusters to $10-$12 per GPU-hour, down from $15-$15.50, in line with deals for large clients such as Anthropic and Google. Anthropic is reportedly not renewing its 50,000-GPU H200 cluster, which SpaceX plans to offer to others at $5 per GPU-hour from early 2027.

The summary adds that analysts still see strong revenue potential from full utilization, and that SpaceX eyes orbital AI satellites by 2027 and 77 gigawatts in orbit by 2031. It is a Grok-written summary of X posts, which X itself warns may contain mistakes, so treat the figures as reported, not confirmed.

stories.headline: Cursor's lauren: we love working on Grok Bot, but Cursor isn't going anywhere
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd and bookmarked it: a direct answer to the question of whether Grok Bot is displacing Cursor.
body: Lauren (@poteto) posted that the team loves working on Grok Bot "but cursor isn't going anywhere," adding that lots of improvements are coming to both and that the teams are cooking. It quote-posts another user's claim that Grok Bot is "light years ahead" in AI bots and that the company has "mostly ditched Cursor."
It is a short statement, with no dates or features, but it is a first-party rebuttal to that narrative from someone on the team.

stories.headline: Tesla Charging for Thanksgiving: 1,027 new stalls across 91 sites in 56 days, plus 29 mobile stalls
stories.why_read: Holiday travel is the stress test for the Supercharger network, and these are the numbers Tesla gave.
body: Tesla Charging says 1,027 stalls across 91 sites opened in the last 56 days, averaging about 18 new stalls a day in the U.S. alone. For the travel window it cites higher uptime and service dispatch, 29 mobile stalls deployed for added capacity, attendants for queue management at the busiest sites, and a waitlist pilot live at 300 sites.
All figures are Tesla's own and cover the preparation, not how the network actually performs under load this weekend.

stories.headline: Mitchell Hashimoto's Rex can resume programs through a server restart, using a new terminal protocol, OSC 7577
stories.why_read: A plain escape-sequence protocol that lets any terminal program restart safely, not just coding agents.
body: Hashimoto says Rex can now resume your programs through a server restart, based on a new terminal protocol, OSC 7577, developed with @herdrdev and reviewed by several terminal emulator and program authors. Because it is ordinary escape sequences, he says any program can restart without special integration or an out-of-band protocol.

Rex ships with built-in support for Claude Code first, emitting OSC 7577 in a session-start hook. He acknowledges that program restart in terminals is "fundamentally unsafe" and says the security ultimately lies in the terminal emulator. Rex uses Lua configuration to opt in program by program, filtering by name, path, working directory or flags, with a one-line off switch.

stories.headline: Hanno Böck: Ubuntu's response to severe kernel flaws is "concerning" and slow
stories.why_read: If you run Ubuntu LTS, the post names specific CVEs that were still unpatched nine days after disclosure.
body: In an oss-security post, Böck says NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288), a remote memory corruption in the Linux TCP stack published November 16, had no Ubuntu fix nine days later, while other distributions had one at disclosure. He also lists a KVM host escape on AMD virtualization (CVE-2026-99312, published November 18) with no fix yet, and a third TCP corruption bug where Ubuntu took multiple weeks.

He argues for expecting fixes within hours, not days, and contrasts Ubuntu's backporting onto an old kernel (7.0.0-44 on a recent LTS) with Debian stable's recent longterm kernel (6.12.118). He suggests everyone should base kernels on upstream longterm releases. He also links a report of possible in-the-wild exploitation.

stories.headline: minipg: PostgreSQL as a single executable, with no server to configure
stories.why_read: Postgres as a file-like .pgdb you can open, dump and run your app against, without Docker or a VM.
body: Jeff Lindsay's minipg ships PostgreSQL as one executable. A .pgdb directory is the database, holding data, config, credentials and the Postgres version, and a server starts when a command needs one and stops when idle. It embeds the postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library, whose Linux personality runs Alpine's Postgres binaries on the host hypervisor with a Plan 9 kernel answering system calls.

Commands include minipg app.pgdb for a psql shell, minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start to run an app with DATABASE_URL set, and dump/restore. The page's in-browser demo downloads about 35 MB and needs JavaScript Promise Integration (Chrome and Edge 137+). The site carries its own warning section, so read it before relying on it.

stories.headline: A bootable x86-64 OS in 24 KB of assembly that runs Qwen3-0.6B with no Linux, libc or C
stories.why_read: An LLM inference stack stripped to the metal: boots in under 100 ms and chats.
body: The llm.asm project's phase 2 is a standalone bootable x86-64 operating system that runs Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B directly on hardware or KVM. The kernel is 24,252 bytes stripped, with 74-94 ms cold boot to an interactive multi-turn chat with a persistent KV cache, all SMP cores online, and the model bound zero-copy from physical RAM.

The README reports 134.9 tok/s decode on QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642, 16 vCPUs) and 55.4 tok/s on a diskless Proxmox VM with a Xeon E5-2670 v3, and token-exact parity with phase 1 across 1 to 32 vCPUs. It needs AVX2, FMA and F16C. These are the author's measurements.

stories.headline: Chips and Cheese: Qualcomm's Oryon 3 reaches the top
stories.why_read: A deep dive on the core that lets an Arm laptop chip challenge the best x86 in CPU performance.
body: Chester Lam writes that Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can now deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition, thanks to the third generation of its in-house Oryon architecture. The chip uses Oryon 3 in both E-core and P-core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls "performance" and "prime" cores.

P-cores outnumber E-cores two to one, an inverted version of Intel's hybrid strategy, and they carry both peak single-thread performance and most multithreaded throughput. The article, dated November 26, goes on to cover the microarchitecture in detail.

stories.headline: A comic on how Lions' Commentary on Unix was copied for 20 years
stories.why_read: A short, funny history of why the best Unix textbook of the 1970s was banned from being a textbook.
body: The FOSS Comics installment explains that in May 1976 John Lions prepared lecture notes on the kernel source of AT&T's Unix Version 6, which became his Unix commentary. By 1977 the notes were circulating among schools and research institutions with Unix licenses, and Bell Labs eventually took over distribution.

At USENIX in June 1979 AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code, and distribution of the book was tightly controlled. The comic leans on Star Wars parody to tell it.

stories.headline: Frontier models vs Google's 2015 code golfers: a 32-problem, 8-language benchmark
stories.why_read: A benchmark with a human baseline that is not a toy: real internal records from a weekly golf contest.
body: The author revived 32 problems from Google's internal go/codegolf contest, where each week's problem was settled by shortest passing program, and gave each model 30 minutes per problem in each of eight languages. The leaderboard scores byte counts, not just whether the code works, giving 256 cells in all.

The HN title says GPT-6.2 Astra is the first model to beat the Googlers' records. I could not run the page's JavaScript leaderboard, so I am reporting that claim as the HN submission's headline, not as a verified score.

stories.headline: Philipp Schmid's five habits he changed for Gemini 4 Neon: fewer rules, skills on demand, handoffs over compaction
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd and bookmarked it: concrete advice on trimming agent setup as models improve.
body: After weeks of running evals with Gemini 4 Neon, Schmid says many guardrails and rules written for older models now slow it down. His five changes: remove strict rules and replace code-style bans with judgment cues; state tool rules once in the tool schema and drop few-shot examples; load skills only when needed instead of large project instruction files; use images and video for reference and to verify output; and hand off context to a new session rather than compacting.

On the last point he says compaction is lossy and breaks the prompt cache, and that he aims for around 500k tokens before compacting even with a 1M-token window. The advice is from his own testing, not a controlled study.

stories.headline: One user's best reasoning-effort setting per model: extra-high for GPT-6.2 and Opus 5.5, high for Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Neon
stories.why_read: If your limits are draining fast, this claims one effort notch is the cause.
body: Arron Knight (@texhnogatsby) lists the best settings as extra-high for GPT-6.2 Astra, GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, and high for Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Neon. He says going one level higher costs 55% to 72% more for 0 to 2 points.
He adds that his own tests found the same and that he builds on high and reviews on extra-high. The numbers come from the chart he posted and his tests, not an independent benchmark.

stories.headline: OpenAI's Tibo: a launch billing mistake under-counted GPT-6.2 usage, so you will hit limits 40% faster on Astra
stories.why_read: If your Codex limits suddenly feel tighter, this is the official reason.
body: Tibo (@thsottiaux) wrote that a billing mistake at the launch of GPT-6.2 incorrectly discounted Astra and Sol usage for most users. After the fix, compared with last week, you will reach limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol, though they still go further than 6 Astra and 6.1 Sol.
Other models were not affected and past usage will not be charged for the difference. As an apology, one banked reset is being added for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro and Business.

stories.headline: Alex Edwards: an overview of Go tooling in 2026
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd it and has a Go learning note; this is a one-stop map of the toolchain.
body: Alex Edwards (@ajmedwards) published a blog post running through Go's available tooling in 2026, covering useful dev tools, code quality tools, testing, profiling, tracing and more.
The X post carries only that description and a link, so I am pointing to it as a reading list item rather than summarizing the contents.

stories.headline: A $0 remote dev box from a Mac mini with Cloudflare Tunnel, Access and Voxl, no open ports
stories.why_read: A clean pattern for reaching a home machine running coding agents from any browser.
body: Fayaz Ahmed describes a roughly one-hour setup. Voxl from Tembo, an open-source screen streamer, listens only on 127.0.0.1; a Cloudflare Tunnel makes the Mac mini connect outward, so no port forwarding or public IP is needed; and Cloudflare Access puts a login wall in front, verified by one-time code or passkey.

Steps include preparing the Mac to run headless (no sleep, auto-start after power loss, auto-login), granting Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, and running cloudflared tunnel login, create and route dns.

stories.headline: Google makes agents use its Workspace MCP servers from Feb 1, 2027, but the Gmail one cannot send email
stories.why_read: If you run agents against Gmail or Drive, the terms and the tool gaps both change.
body: Tech Stackups reports that on November 24 Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and added a clause: from February 1, 2027, any tool that is or is driven by an AI agent must reach Workspace through those servers. The Gmail server can search, read threads, create drafts and manage labels, but sending, replying, forwarding and editing drafts require partner access.

Agents calling REST APIs directly would be held to Standard-tier quotas, and the addendum caps retention of derived data such as embeddings at 30 days and bans training on the data. Docs, Slides and Tasks are near parity with REST; Gmail and Drive are thinner.

stories.headline: Grok Bot team publishes 19 playbooks for building teams of specialized bots
stories.why_read: The official copy-and-paste workflows for sales, marketing, engineering and more, from the Grok Bot team itself.
body: X's news summary says SpaceXAI released 19 detailed playbooks for building teams of specialized AI bots, taken from internal setups, covering sales, marketing, engineering and legal ops with real prompts. Grok Bot lets users create named bots on shared cloud computers that sign into apps, hand work to one another and run on schedules.

Engineer Lauren Tan's example org is one chief of staff, three managers and 16 workers, and team member Evan Bacon asked for feedback on the biggest problems. Skeptics worry about cost and whether Grok models match rivals like Claude. It is a summary of posts and may be wrong.

stories.headline: New US rules on Nvidia H100-class rentals push Zhipu's GLM-5.5 and Moonshot's Kimi K4 later
stories.why_read: Export controls reaching into overseas rented compute change the open-model release cadence.
body: X's news summary says that since November 19 new US rules require licenses for overseas data centers renting large-scale H100-equivalent compute to Chinese firms. Zhipu AI's GLM-5.5, aimed at a 3-trillion-parameter November release, now eyes early 2027 or later, partly due to tighter controls on distillation from OpenAI and Anthropic models.

Moonshot's Kimi K4 faces a six-to-twelve-month gap between releases as it loses overseas compute access and shifts to alternatives such as Google and Meta models, per the same summary. It is an auto-generated summary of X posts, so treat details as reported.

stories.headline: Apollo chart: Magnificent Seven revenue per employee hits $780,000 vs about $500,000 for the rest of the S&P
stories.why_read: A sober data point on where AI payoff is and is not showing up.
body: Per X's news summary, an Apollo Global Management chart shows inflation-adjusted revenue per employee for big tech climbing since 2023 while the S&P 493 stays flat, with profit margins expanding for tech leaders and steady near 10 percent elsewhere. Apollo economist Torsten Slok is quoted as saying AI investment has brought zero financial gains to non-tech corporate America so far.
Observers debate whether productivity will eventually spread more widely. This is a summary of posts about the chart, not the chart itself.

stories.headline: Ron Baron compares Musk to Michael Jordan and says SpaceX has a fast edge in AI data centers
stories.why_read: A big, long-time SpaceX and Tesla holder's view of the AI-compute thesis.
body: X's news summary says investor Ron Baron, a backer of SpaceX and Tesla since 2017, called Musk a super engineer, physicist and entrepreneur, and estimated AI data center projects at $35 billion per gigawatt with quick returns from leases to hyperscalers such as Anthropic, which has a $1.25 billion monthly deal through 2029.

Musk replied humbly, crediting his teams, and Baron said he picked up a new Model Y amid strong Full Self-Driving demand. Investor commentary from a long-time holder, so read it as sentiment, not analysis.

stories.headline: Musk: every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from him
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd it; the post is a one-line promise with no mechanics yet.
body: Elon Musk posted: "Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally." The post itself gives no details on eligibility, timing, account structure or cost.
Treat it as an announcement to watch: nothing in the post says how shares would be delivered or what regulatory steps are needed.

stories.headline: Musk predicts robots will outnumber humans, as Optimus hammering clips turn out to be AI-generated
stories.why_read: A reminder to check the clip before the claim.
body: X's news summary says Musk told the World Economic Forum earlier this year that robotics and AI would lead to more robots than people. Viral clips of a Tesla Optimus robot hammering nails sparked excitement, though several posts noted they were AI-generated.
The summary adds that Tesla has begun early Optimus production at its Fremont factory with customer deliveries planned for late next year. It reflects X chatter and may contain errors.

stories.headline: Why hasn't AI built a better Windows yet?
stories.why_read: A lively thread on the gap between generating code and shipping an OS.
body: X's news summary says the discussion asks why, with millions of developers and billions in AI investment, no one has topped Windows, which still powers over 70% of desktops. Replies point to testing, hardware drivers, security and ecosystem building as work AI cannot yet fully handle.
Humans remain essential for oversight on complex projects, while early experiments such as Tilo and Omarchy are mentioned as AI-assisted alternatives. It is a summary of posts and may be wrong.

stories.headline: Mark Cuban asks Grok to write a universal health care plan with zero out-of-pocket and the lowest taxpayer cost
stories.why_read: A famous prompt, plus his own question about whether he could have written it better.
body: Mark Cuban posted a prompt asking @grok, "with no preconceived notions," to write a plan covering all US residents with the best available care at no cost out of pocket at the time of scheduling or receiving it, at the lowest possible cost to taxpayers and employers.

He also asked that it maximize earnings for doctors and nurses while paying hospitals, clinics and other providers enough to at worst break even, using common sense as the constraint, and invited Grok to critique the prompt. The post contains the prompt only; the plan itself is not in it.

stories.headline: Why Colorado has exactly ten times Wyoming's population despite looking like twins on a map
stories.why_read: A neat 2020 census fact and a thread to explain it.
body: Iain Cameron notes that in the 2020 census Colorado had 5.77 million people and Wyoming 577,000, exactly ten times as many, though the two states look like enormous rectangular neighbours. His thread (1/n) sets out to explain why.
The X post gives the numbers and the question; the explanation is in the thread that follows.

stories.headline: An app for learning electricity step by step: 37 lessons in 21 languages
stories.why_read: Anand RT'd it: a physics-for-everyday-life explainer for how home electricity works and stays safe.
body: Dilum Sanjaya says he made an app for learning electricity, covering how everyday things in your home work, what keeps you safe, and a few tricks that "feel like magic." The post says it has 37 lessons in 21 languages and includes a demo video.
That is the extent of the post, so quality is untested here.
